For n≥2 nonzero embeddings, let u_i=E_i/||E_i|| and c average cosine over distinct pairs. Direct algebra gives ||mean(u)||²=[1+(n−1)c]/n, hence −1/(n−1)≤c≤1 and (n−2)/[2(n−1)]≤g≤1. For five items, g≥0.375: the gate cannot close. Orthogonal items give g=0.5. The identity applies to unit embeddings; unequal raw norms break the equivalence. Mask padding, exclude diagonal pairs, and specify singleton/empty-history behavior.

With unit embeddings, residual magnitude is |alpha|g√([1+(n−1)c]/n): coherence already increases the mean’s magnitude, so gating compounds that effect. Unrestricted alpha can become negative, subtracting the history direction. At alpha=0, residual-branch gradients into embeddings and g vanish, while ∂L/∂alpha can be nonzero. Subsequently, shared embeddings can adjust angles to manipulate g and norms to amplify the residual; cosine’s scale invariance does not remove norm-dependent optimization effects ([The Hidden Pitfalls of the Cosine Similarity Loss](https://openreview.net/pdf?id=yO9i3SD8hN)).

Useful controls: normalize each item before pooling; separately test normalizing the pooled direction with an epsilon threshold, recording near-zero means. Compare learned gating against g=1, matched constant gates, and gates shuffled within history-length groups. Ablate stop-gradient on g alone, the pooled vector alone, and both; detaching g blocks direct gate gradients but shared encoder/scorer updates still change its geometry. Frozen reference embeddings provide a stronger control. Track alpha, norms, c, g, residual/base norm ratios, and validation HR@10. Stop-gradient is an optimization intervention, not evidence of semantic gating ([SimSiam](https://arxiv.org/abs/2011.10566)).
